title: Shelly’s new smart valve shuts off your home’s water before a leak becomes a flood
author: Andrew Liszewski
content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After releasing a $28 leak sensor earlier this year that conveniently runs off a battery for two years, Shelly is announcing an accompanying smart valve you can install on your home’s main water line to automatically turn off the flow when one of those sensors detects a problem. The Shelly Neo Smart Water Valve is available now through the company’s online store for $499.99, plus the cost of installation if you don’t trust your plumbing skills. It’s not a cheap solution, but it’s cheaper than the fallout of a leak turning into a disaster.

The Neo Smart Water Valve is designed to be installed on a standard US 1-inch thread connection (the company plans to launch additional size options next year) and is made from brass so it’s safe to use on plumbing carrying drinking water. It has an IPX7 waterproof rating so the valve will keep working if flooding means it ends up submerged. However, the valve lacks a battery of its own and requires a connection to a power source through an included USB adapter cable. Connecting it to a waterproof power bank instead of an outlet may be the best approach to ensure it still works during a power outage.

The smart valve connects to other devices over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth and is designed to integrate into existing smart home setups using webhooks, MQTT, or scripting for advanced users. In addition to shutting off the flow of water into your home in about 12 seconds, the valve also features an ultrasonic measurement system that tracks pressure, flow rate, your home’s consumption, and even the temperature of the water. Through the Shelly app, you can monitor all of that data in order to spot unusual usage patterns that could indicate a wasteful leak, or ensure the pressure doesn’t get high enough to damage pipes or appliances.

title: Powerful storm threatens East Coast with hurricane-level flooding, damaging winds
author: Abc News
content:
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed due to the weather threat.

A Mill Valley resident and her child look at a flooded area in Mill Valley, California, US, November 24, 2026.

A Mill Valley resident and her child look at a flooded area in Mill Valley, California, US, November 24, 2026.

A Mill Valley resident and her child look at a flooded area in Mill Valley, California, US, November 24, 2026.

A Mill Valley resident and her child look at a flooded area in Mill Valley, California, US, November 24, 2026.

More than 80 million people from Georgia to Massachusetts are under wind alerts as a powerful storm takes shape on the East Coast, bringing the threat of damaging winds, significant coastal flooding, and heavy rain to the area.

Significant coastal flooding is expected along much of the East Coast Wednesday and Thursday as the storm tears through, pushing strong onshore winds against already elevated water levels from king tides.

The weather threat prompted the postponement of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City. The parade will now take place Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, according to Macy's.

A Mill Valley resident and her child look at a flooded area in Mill Valley, California, US, November 24, 2026. Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul issued a state of emergency for New York City and Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties. In, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a statewide state of emergency across the state that went into effect at 6 p.m. ET on Wednesday.

The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for New York City from 10 a.m. Thursday to 1 a.m. Friday and a coastal flood warning for the entire city from 7 a.m. Thursday into Friday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a news conference about the postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, in New York. Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo

The worst of the storm is expected Thursday afternoon into the late evening with steady winds of 30 to 40 mph and wind gusts up to 65 mph possible, according to the New York City Emergency Management Department.

The heaviest rain is expected from midday to midnight and widespread street flooding is possible, the department said.

Major coastal flooding is also expected in Atlantic City, New Jersey, on Thanksgiving morning, when an 8 a.m. high tide is forecast to reach 8.2 feet. The record high is 9 feet.

The Thanksgiving holiday coastal storm is expected to bring flooding and high winds along the East Coast. ABC News

The storm is expected to bring wind gusts of up to 70 mph along the New Jersey shore and 50 to 60 mph inland throughout Thanksgiving Day. Parts of the state could receive between 1 and 4 inches of rain.

Cape May, Atlantic and Ocean counties face the greatest risk of flooding. Officials say the worst conditions are expected Thursday morning, when strong winds will coincide with high tide. The worst of the winds will occur through the afternoon.

The state of emergency does not restrict travel but will allow state and local agencies to coordinate more quickly on emergency response efforts, including road closures and traffic control, according to officials.

Rainfall amounts that are expected from the Thanksgiving holiday storm. ABC News

Officials warned that high winds could knock down trees and power lines, leaving some residents without electricity into the weekend. Strong winds may also prevent utility crews from safely using bucket trucks to repair damaged lines.

The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities said electric companies are positioning crews and equipment throughout the state and bringing in additional support. However, officials cautioned that dangerous wind conditions could delay power restoration.

Potentially damaging winds are expected along the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day, November 26, 2026 ABC News

According to NOAA, water levels above 8 feet can cause severe flooding, including structural damage and widespread roadway flooding across New Jersey in Brigantine, Atlantic City, Ventnor and Pleasantville. Vulnerable homes and businesses could be severely damaged or destroyed as water levels rise further above that threshold and numerous roads could become impassable, with some neighborhoods potentially becoming isolated.

Coastal flooding and high wind warnings have been issued along the East Coast. ABC News

Floodwaters could also pose a danger to anyone attempting to cross them on foot or in a vehicle as minor to moderate high tide flooding is expected to continue up the coast through southern Maine Thursday morning. Long Island, for example, could see up to 3 feet of flood inundation at high tide.

Meanwhile, heavy rain and strengthening winds moved across the Southeast Wednesday as the storm developed. Strong onshore flow and above-average water temperatures are expected to contribute to abundant moisture and potentially flooding rainfall.

In Charleston, South Carolina, major coastal flooding inundated parts of the city Wednesday morning.

Flooding impacts could become more extensive along the southeast South Carolina coast, including erosion at area beaches and limited or no access to docks, piers and some islands.

Rain is expected to spread across the region Wednesday, from Memphis, Tennessee, to Charleston, South Carolina, and Norfolk, Virginia.

A Level 2 out of 4 flood threat is in place from Charleston to Norfolk. Heavy rain could fall at rates of up to 1.5 inches per hour, potentially triggering flash flooding. Rainfall totals could reach 3 to 6 inches across the area, with the heaviest rain expected to begin Wednesday afternoon and continue into the night.

On Thursday, a Level 2 out of 4 flood threat is in place from the Delmarva Peninsula to New York City and the Tri-State area as periods of heavy rain could lead to isolated instances of flash flooding, with rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches possible.

The strongest winds are expected to arrive in Philadelphia Thursday morning and in New York City during the afternoon.

A high wind warning is in place for both cities, with gusts of up to 60 mph possible. Along the immediate coast, gusts could reach 70 mph. and the winds could bring down trees and power lines.

Rain is expected to reach Philadelphia between 3 a.m. and 6 a.m. Thursday and continue throughout the day and evening. In New York City, rain is expected to arrive between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m. and also continue throughout the day and evening.

The storm is expected to continue up the coast, reaching Boston between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. Thursday with rain expected to spread into Buffalo and Chicago on Thanksgiving.

title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.

Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.

Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.

"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.

He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.

The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.

The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.

The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.

Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.

"It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.

The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.

title: OpenAI CFO says blue tsunami ‘didn’t dramatically change’ IPO plans
author: Brent D. Griffiths
content:
The 2026 midterms haven't changed OpenAI's IPO plans, OpenAI chief financial officer Sarah Friar says.

"Look, we are paid as operators to manage scenarios," Friar said on Friday during a live interview on CNBC. "I don't think there was something that dramatically changed for us."

Friar referred back to OpenAI's previous plans to target an IPO sometime next year. All eyes are on Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, and whether it will forge ahead with an IPO, perhaps as soon as this month.

Democrats turned in a generational-level rout of Republicans in the midterm elections, not only flipping control of Congress but coming into the new year with healthy majorities. At the state level, Democratic candidates flipped governorships in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio after running on promises of reining in new data center development.

Friar said OpenAI, which is trying to rebrand data centers as "compute campuses," will continue to invest in the sprawling facilities that are central to both OpenAI and the broader AI industry's future.

"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," she said. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital."

On Thursday, OpenAI announced what it called "a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure." Under its pledge, OpenAI said it would pay the full cost of the electricity it uses and any necessary grid improvements, do away with non-disclosure agreements with public officials (with narrow exceptions), and publish data on the jobs it expects to create.

"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," she said.

Friar said that OpenAI's business remains healthy. She said that in the third quarter, OpenAI's revenue grew 70%, including a doubling of its enterprise sales. She said that OpenAI's latest private funding round is at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, though she likely misspoke and meant $1.25 trillion. In March, OpenAI announced that it had closed a funding round at an $852 billion post-money valuation.

"I genuinely think that is a good indication of our Q3 momentum and how that momentum carries into 2027," Friar said.

Friar said one reason she's excited for an IPO is because a market debut would be in line with OpenAI's mission to ensure artificial intelligence for all.

"I personally feel very driven to put that economic value creation that's happening into as many hands as we can," she said. "Like, why should it just be limited to institutions?"

title: Progressives want new Democratic leaders. The party's landslide complicates that.
author: Https
content:
By Corbin Trent’s estimate, he’s spending 15 hours a day on a cause that has animated the left ever since Democrats won huge majorities in the House and Senate: urging them to dump their leaders.

Trent, a former spokesman for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has some well-known allies in his long-shot campaign to oust Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. They include actor Mark Ruffalo, former Ocasio-Cortez chief of staff Saikat Chakrabarti, and countless progressive influencers.

But they don’t include Ocasio-Cortez, who underscored on Tuesday that she’s backing Jeffries. Even Trent acknowledged that what legions of online progressives are asking for — the rejection of leaders who just presided over Democratic landslides — is unlikely to happen.

“I reckon it’s about a 10% chance on Schumer and a 3% chance on Jeffries,” Trent told Semafor. “What matters, and matters a lot, is making it loud and clear that voters asked for something else. That it is being denied to them. If you’ve ever got a chance to beat these folks, you need votes.”

AD

Theoretically, the votes to shake up leadership are at least within reach. Informal whip counts and hallway interviews confirm that dozens of newly elected Democrats are interested in challengers to the two New Yorkers who occasionally break from the left. But realistically, the battle to replace Jeffries and Schumer was built for a disappointing election, not a landslide.

And the obstacles of the anti-leadership campaign are revealing the limited reach of a progressive movement that wants to pick the next presidential nominee. Critics of Schumer haven’t given up on enlisting Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen to challenge him, but no Democrat has stepped up to take on Jeffries.

Even if Van Hollen mounts a campaign, it will be a massive uphill climb for progressives to deny Schumer the votes in next month’s closed-door vote. The left’s chances of defeating Jeffries are even lower.

AD

But by forcing the question, progressives hope to either pull off a miracle — or at least, keep an argument going. Activists believe that they, not Schumer and Jeffries, put in the work to win the biggest Democratic victories in decades. The progressive media outlets that exploded after the party’s 2024 loss to Trump are now watching the leaders take credit for what they think their movement built.

Their message is consistent: That voters who want “change” and support progressive ideas will stay engaged only if the leadership changes and President Donald Trump is forced to veto big progressive bills.

At last week’s post-election Crooked Con, a gathering of progressive activists, strategists, influencers, and podcast addicts, the demand for new leaders hung in the air. Attendees walking up to the Washington Convention Center on Saturday were offered leaflets about stopping bipartisan permitting reform moving through the Senate, warning that it would speed up the building of “immigrant detention centers.” (The bill advanced two days later.)

AD

Inside, there were excited murmurs whenever a Democrat was asked about replacing Schumer or Jeffries.

Pressed by Pod Save America co-host Jon Lovett on whether she would challenge Schumer, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin gave a winding answer that didn’t rule it out — but suggested that Schumer could win her over.

“Look, if he wants to be majority leader, what is your plan for the first 100 days?” she said. “How are you going to do things differently so that Democrats get their sh*t together?”

That got muted applause from an audience ready to join an insurgency. There was much more excitement when Rep.-elect Milat Kiros of Colorado said there had been a “mandate” for change, not for current leadership; Kiros unseated Rep. Diana DeGette in one of the left’s biggest primary wins.

Everywhere he went, Van Hollen was asked if he would challenge Schumer. In a short interview with Semafor, he disputed the idea that the leader had earned the job already by electing between seven and nine new Democratic senators.

“I’m glad that the DSCC and Senate Majority PAC raised a lot of money,” Van Hollen told Semafor. “I mean, their Republican counterparts raised even more money. I think the lesson from this election was, this was people power over money.”

The scale of the Democratic wins has made the entire push trickier.

“Look, we had a wonderful, wonderful outcome,” said Maurice Mitchell, the president of the Working Families Party, which clashed with DC Democrats over primaries in the Midwest and California. “It’s almost like it would be greedy of me to want better outcomes. But I know there were elections that could have been won if we were able to move as a united front.”

title: Nepal’s fight to rebuild after flood disaster
content:
101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a devastating natural disaster.

On the morning of August 26, 2026, a devastating flash flood of rock and ice thundered from a high Himalayan mountain through Nepal’s valleys, sweeping away homes, villages and bridges.

At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing.

It was the latest in a series of natural disasters that have battered Nepal in recent years as climate change accelerates.

This programme follows the rescuers risking their lives to search for the missing and those providing aid and refuge for traumatised children and families.

title: Northeastern Florida faces flood threats from devastating storms
author: Abc News
content:
Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday

By DAVE COLLINS Associated Press , KATHY MCCORMACK Associated Press , and JOHN RA Associated Press

Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.

The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).

“Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected,” the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. “In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger.”

The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.

Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.

The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May.

“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.

In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.

Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.

___

Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.
